title: The missing layer: decision integrity as a verifiable assurance layer in interpretive clinical artificial intelligence.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] Interpretive clinical artificial intelligence (AI), in which a clinician interprets an image or signal and an AI system offers a competing or confirming read, is increasingly routine in radiology, pathology, dermatology, and endoscopy. Oversight of these systems assumes that independent human judgment occurred before AI influence entered the decision. The informatics infrastructure, meaning the electronic health record, its audit logs, and the reporting systems built on them, does not verify this. We name the missing assurance layer decision integrity, situate it between cybersecurity verification and clinical quality review, and argue it is a measurement construct distinct from diagnostic accuracy. Drawing on the logic of preregistration, we propose a candidate architecture, a minimal six-event record under sequential disclosure, preserving tamper-evident evidence of pre-AI judgment, post-AI revision, and rationale. The architecture is a candidate for evaluation, not a validated standard; its purpose is to make clinician independence auditable rather than assumed.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models in Surgical Shared Decision-Making and Informed Consent: A Narrative Review.
desc: [Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland)] Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) may make surgical information easier to access and understand. However, these tools cannot replace the clinician's role in shared decision-making or the requirements for valid informed consent. Methods: This narrative review follows the surgical patient pathway from diagnosis and explanation to option comparison, shared decision-making, and informed consent. It examines conventional digital tools, LLM-assisted communication, personalized prediction, direct consent studies, patient and professional perspectives and legal, ethical, and governance issues. A formal meta-analysis and study-level risk-of-bias assessment were not performed. Results: AI may support several stages of surgical care. Diagnostic and predictive systems can assist clinicians. LLMs can help explain approved information, prepare patients for consultation, and improve consent materials. Conventional interactive tools have the strongest evidence for better comprehension. Evidence for LLM-assisted consent is still based mainly on simulations and document analyses. Patient-facing use requires source control, privacy protection, and visible clinical oversight. AI cannot establish capacity, voluntariness, or final authorization. We propose a five-level framework in which safeguards increase with clinical influence. Conclusions: AI may support the patient's path from diagnosis to an informed surgical choice when it uses approved information, serves a defined task, and remains under clinical oversight. Current evidence does not support autonomous AI-mediated consent or AI-directed treatment choice. The aim should be a better-informed, preference-sensitive decision, not an automated signature.

title: Safety, Feasibility, and Acceptability of the MINERVA Voice Conversational Agent for Emergency Department History-Taking
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; conditions: History Taking, Artificial Intelligence (AI); type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 250; status: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] This study evaluates whether an artificial intelligence (AI) conversational agent called MINERVA (Medical Interface for Navigating the Emergency Room with Voice Assistance) can safely and feasibly gather medical histories from emergency department (ED) patients and produce accurate summaries. The main questions it aims to answer are: Can an AI conversational agent gather and summarize patient histories in the emergency department? Are the resulting summaries accurate? Do they capture essential clinical information? Can an AI agent overseeing these conversations independently identify red-flag symptoms that may need time-sensitive clinical interventions? Adult ED patients interact with MINERVA via either voice chat or typing on a keyboard. MINERVA asks them questions about their symptoms and generates a summary which the patients review for accuracy. MINERVA reviews the conversation for clinical red flags that suggest urgent evaluation is required. Participants fill out a survey providing feedback on their experience. The summary is not saved in the medical record and clinical care is not affected. Physician reviewers will evaluate the safety, accuracy, and clinical value of the MINERVA interview transcripts and summaries using standardized rubrics, including whether MINERVA was correct in identifying red-flag symptoms that may need time-sensitive clinical interventions.

title: AI-Driven, Timing-Aware Power Optimization
desc: Post-route power recovery changes cell choices under tightly coupled timing, electrical and physical constraints, and the value of each change depends on what it costs to repair its side effects. We propose an AI-driven framework in which a learned model drives both phases of the optimization: it ranks the powerrecovery edits to try and the repair actions that follow, while deterministic electronic design automation (EDA) analyses govern every acceptance. The framework records baseline constraint margins, identifies the damage a recovery transaction introduces in each analysis view, holds pre-existing violations at their baseline rather than working them inside the power step, and caps repair spending at a fraction of the measured saving. An ensemble of gradient-boosted models predicts power change, normalized damage reduction and constraint-regression risk from action and timing-context features available before each trial; calibrated, conservative estimates feed separate acquisition scores for recovery and repair, with a deterministic fallback when the model is uncertain. Recovery and repair remain speculative until physical implementation and fresh analysis establish baseline preservation and positive net saving. We specify the contract, the learned policy, the transactional flow and a pre-registered public evaluation protocol on open designs. Evidence from a companion study on public designs supports the contract; the learned policy is proposed, and no trained-model results or proprietary design measurements are reported.

title: Facilitating Valid Statistical Inference in Biomedical Image Synthesis
desc: Generative AI for medical image synthesis is increasingly used to impute missing data and augment biomedical datasets. Yet despite achieving high computational similarity to their real-world counterparts, synthetic images remain uncommon in clinical research practice, in part because of concerns about their biological validity. Here, we evaluate whether synthetic images support reliable downstream statistical analysis and biological inference in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and multiplexed immunofluorescence (mIF) imaging. We find that associations between patient phenotypes and synthesized images can be severely attenuated. This is because synthesis methods typically omit clinically relevant covariates and therefore generate images that, although visually realistic, mask key biological differences. Furthermore, naive analyses treat synthesized images as if they were observed, ignoring the statistical uncertainty introduced by synthesis. Drawing on multiple imputation theory, we introduce Phenotype Aware Multiple Synthesis (PAMS), an analysis framework that requires no model retraining and instead adjusts synthesized output to recover valid biological estimates with appropriately calibrated uncertainty. Applied to MRI and mIF data, PAMS reduced estimation bias and restored nominal confidence interval coverage. Because it is compatible with existing synthesis pipelines, PAMS offers a practical and rigorous route to statistically and biologically valid use of synthesized images in biomedical imaging research.

title: ChronIQ-DRx2: restoring unwritten clinical decision logic unlocks personalized chronic disease management
desc: Clinical records routinely document medical interventions but often omit the reasoning connecting patient-specific evidence to medical action. This limits the decision-relevant supervision available for training models for personalized care. Here we evaluate a data-augmentation approach that makes selected clinical decision relationships explicit in an 8-billion-parameter Qwen3 model, ChronIQ-DRx2. Using the same training cases and model architecture, expert-guided logic reconstruction was applied across four chronic diseases. On the held-out evaluation, the enhanced model had the highest plotted end-to-end task-completion rate among evaluated systems and higher plotted scores across diagnostic, medication and follow-up measures. The serious clinical error rates shown were 16.7% for the baseline and 12.5% for the enhanced model. In the human-AI evaluation, physician accuracy was 87.40% alone and 88.20% with AI assistance, while mean completion time was 0.959 and 0.780 min, respectively; medical-student accuracy was 62.71% and 74.80%, and mean completion time was 0.210 and 0.195 min. These results are descriptive point estimates; inferential comparisons are not reported here. Structured outputs may make recommendations easier to review, but rationale faithfulness, generalizability and effects on clinical safety require further evaluation.

EGFR-targeted antibody−toxin conjugate in recurrent glioma: a phase 1 trial
desc: D2C7-ATC is a recombinant antibody−toxin conjugate (ATC) targeting wild-type epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and mutant EGFR variant III (EGFRvIII). We conducted a single-arm, single-site, open-label phase 1 trial evaluating a single infusion of D2C7-ATC via convection-enhanced delivery in the enhancing disease of 81 patients with biopsy-confirmed recurrent malignant glioma. The primary objective was to determine toxicity and the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) of D2C7-ATC. Secondary objectives included describing overall survival (OS) and assessing the association between EGFR expression and OS. The median overall survival (mOS) was 7.9 months among 72 patients with isocitrate dehydrogenase wild-type recurrent glioblastoma (IDHwt rGBM), including 35 patients in the dose-escalation stage (40 to 35,032 ng ml^−1) and 37 patients in the dose-expansion stage (RP2D of 6,920 ng ml^−1). D2C7-ATC was generally well tolerated, with mainly grade 1−2 treatment-related adverse events (67%). The maximum tolerated dose was exceeded at 35,032 ng ml^−1, where four patients experienced dose-limiting toxicities, including grade 4 ( N = 2) and grade 3 ( N = 2) events. Eight patients died on trial; all deaths were unrelated to D2C7-ATC. Univariate analyses identified survival-associated biomarkers, including tumor D2C7 antibody reactivity, circulating cytokines, a tumor inflammatory gene signature and neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes in blood. Notably, patients with IDHwt rGBM with a D2C7 antibody reactivity score of <1.5+ in pre-treatment tumor had an mOS of 17.38 months, whereas those with low IL-8 in post-treatment plasma had an mOS of 16.6 months. These findings indicate that EGFR-targeted D2C7-ATC therapy prolongs survival in a subset of patients with IDHwt rGBM via intratumoral and systemic immune activation. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02303678 . Results of a phase 1 trial of the antibody−toxin conjugate D2C7-ATC targeting EGFR/EGFRvIII in patients with recurrent malignant glioma show encouraging safety and efficacy signals, with translational analyses of patient samples indicating intratumoral and systemic immune activation.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Chronic Rhinosinusitis: From Molecular Profiling to Personalized Clinical Management-A Systematic Review.
source: PubMed · International journal of molecular sciences
desc: [International journal of molecular sciences] Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is a heterogeneous inflammatory disease imposing a substantial health and economic burden. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to address CRS complexity in both clinical and research settings. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines, searching PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase for peer-reviewed articles utilizing machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing, with a focus on molecular-level or immunologic mechanisms in CRS. Thirty-one studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Our results demonstrate that while AI-driven analysis helps stratify patient endotypes, the identified schemes exhibit substantial heterogeneity in cluster numbers and features, raising concerns about their reproducibility. AI applications also included histopathological image interpretation, drug discovery, biologic therapy selection, and prognostic modeling to evaluate revision surgery risks and olfactory dysfunction. However, using the PROBAST+AI framework, we found that 87.1% of the assessed studies carry a high overall risk of bias, mainly due to the reliance on apparent performance or internal validation and limited independent evaluation of model performance, indicating that many reported performance estimates may be optimistic. Future large-scale, multicenter collaborations integrating AI into clinical workflows will be essential to establish reliable and generalizable AI applications for personalized CRS management.

title: AI-Supported CBT-Based Psychoeducation for Caregivers of Individuals With Schizophrenia
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Kastamonu University; conditions: Schizophrenia Caregiver, Caregiver Burden, Emotional Expressivity; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 88; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Schizophrenia is a chronic mental disorder that affects the diagnosed individual and the family members involved in the care process from a biopsychosocial perspective. The course of the illness, the recurrence of symptoms, and the high level of care required can increase the burden on caregivers and make it difficult for them to express their emotions. Structured psychoeducation and cognitive-behavioral interventions have been reported to be beneficial for caregivers in managing these challenges. The aim of this study is to develop an AI-supported psychoeducation program based on a cognitive-behavioral approach for caregivers of individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia and to evaluate the program's impact on caregiving burden and the level of emotional expression. The six-week program will cover topics such as the caregiver role and burden, schizophrenia, the thought-emotion-behavior cycle, recognizing and expressing emotions, effective communication, setting boundaries, seeking support, signs of relapse, and crisis planning. Content based on scientific literature will be evaluated by experts. Artificial intelligence will facilitate interaction with the content, participation in activities, the application of skills, and structured feedback. The system will not provide clinical assessments, diagnoses, or personalized treatment recommendations; participants will be referred to appropriate healthcare services in situations requiring professional evaluation. The study will be conducted using a quasi-experimental design with pre-test and post-test control groups. A total of 88 caregivers will be recruited, with 44 assigned to the experimental group and 44 to the control group. The program will be administered to the experimental group, while the control group will receive routine care. Data will be collected using the Caregiver Descriptive Information Form, the Zarit Caregiver Burden Scale, and the Emotional Expression Scale. A Program Evaluation Form will also be used for the experimental group. The program to be developed is expected to reduce the caregiving burden on caregivers and improve their ability to express emotions. It is anticipated that the findings will contribute to psychiatric nursing practice, the development of AI-supported psychoeducation programs, and the strengthening of psychosocial support provided to caregivers.

title: MOFI reveals dynamic multi-omics coordination during cell fate progression
desc: Cell fate decisions are shaped by dynamic coordination across transcriptomic, chromatin, and protein layers. Time-series single-cell multi-omics assays now enable these molecular layers to be profiled across developmental stages, yet each cell is still observed only once, and the continuous multi-omics trajectories connecting discrete snapshots remain unresolved. A central challenge is therefore to jointly integrate paired omics measurements while reconstructing their shared developmental progression. Here we present Multi-Omics Fate Inference (MOFI), a dynamically constrained multi-omics integration framework designed to reconstruct continuous cell fate transitions from paired multi-omics snapshots sampled across multiple time points. MOFI jointly models omics-specific state dynamics, cross-omics correspondence, and shared population growth within a unified framework, enabling cross-omics perturbation response analysis and identification of candidate cross-omics transformation programs. Across simulated benchmarks and paired RNA-ATAC/RNA-protein time-series datasets, MOFI reconstructed continuous fate transitions, population dynamics and cross-omics changes consistent with observed measurements. In kidney organoids, MOFI captured coordinated RNA-ATAC progression of nephron lineage specification. In hematopoietic progenitors, MOFI predicted perturbation-responsive lineage redistribution and nominated multi-omics transformation programs linking transcriptional modules with protein-level responses. In neural developmental systems, MOFI resolved gradual brain organoid maturation and interneuron lineage allocation during human cortical development. Together, MOFI provides a dynamics-grounded method for converting discrete paired multi-omics snapshots into interpretable models of cell fate progression, perturbation response, and cross-omics transformation analysis.

title: BanglaDiaHallu: Hallucinations of large language models and the effect of guideline-grounded retrieval-augmented generation in Bangla diabetes question answering
desc: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for health advice, but they can produce fluent statements that are false or unsupported, known as hallucinations, and this risk is poorly characterised in low-resource languages such as Bangla. We measured hallucinations of locally deployable open-weight LLMs in Bangla diabetes question answering and tested whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounded in Bangladeshs National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus reduces them. Forty patient questions spanning six clinical sub-domains were each answered twice, under zero-shot prompting, by Qwen3.5-9B, TigerLLM-9B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, and by BanglaDiaRAG, which adds hybrid dense (BGE-M3) and sparse (BM25) retrieval from a physician-reviewed Bangla guideline knowledge base to Qwen3.5-9B. Two physicians rated the 400 de-identified responses by consensus for medical accuracy, completeness, safety, readability and reliability on a 0-1 scale, and responses with accuracy below 0.70 were classified as hallucinated. Hallucination rates were 2.5% for Gemma-4-26B-A4B, 3.8% for TigerLLM-9B, 22.5% for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 77.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Guideline grounding lowered the rate of Qwen3.5-9B to 11.3% (difference -66.3 percentage points; 95% CI -76.3 to -55.0) and raised every criterion by 0.24 to 0.38 points (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). BanglaDiaRAG outscored Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on all five criteria and matched or exceeded TigerLLM-9B, but it remained below Gemma-4-26B-A4B in safety, readability and reliability, and its residual errors were specific, confident and potentially harmful. Guideline grounding can turn a weak general-purpose model into a much safer Bangla diabetes assistant, but the choice of base model mattered as much as retrieval and no configuration was free of hallucination, so clinical oversight remains essential before patient-facing use.

title: Advancing Cancer Biomarker Discovery Through Multi-Omics, Bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review.
desc: [Proteomics] The rapid accumulation of multi-omics data provides increasing opportunities for cancer biomarker discovery, but the heterogeneity and high dimensionality of these datasets remain major challenges for data integration and analysis. This review examines the application of bioinformatics and artificial intelligence for multi-omics integration in cancer biomarker research. Common multi-omics data paradigms and integration strategies are discussed, followed by a review of the bioinformatics, machine learning and deep learning approaches applied across 84 included studies. Cross-study comparison showed limited recurrence among the reported biomarkers, with only 15 biomarkers identified in at least four studies. Further assessment of the 13 recurrent protein-coding biomarkers showed significant protein-protein interaction enrichment and functional convergence in cancer-related processes, particularly PI3K/AKT and ERBB2-related signaling. This review also highlights current challenges, including missing data, heterogeneity across datasets, limited independent validation and the interpretability of artificial intelligence models. Future research may benefit from integrating multi-omics data with clinical information, pathological imaging, electronic health records, single-cell multi-omics and radiomics, together with broader datasets and greater use of independent validation to support the translation of multi-omics biomarker findings into clinical applications.

title: Balanced Risk Integrity Index: a stratum-level metric for evaluating clinical prediction alerts under competing risks and censoring
desc: Background: Conventional discrimination metrics, such as the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), do not characterize the composition of outcomes among patients flagged as high risk by clinical prediction models. This limitation is particularly relevant in critical care, where competing deaths and incomplete follow-up can complicate the interpretation of prediction alerts. We developed the Balanced Risk Integrity Index (BRII), a stratum-level metric defined as the proportion of target events among target events, competing deaths, and early-censored observations in a flagged high-risk stratum. BRII is algebraically related to positive predictive value (PPV) and is reported alongside its component decomposition to characterize the outcome composition of flagged patients. Methods: We evaluated BRII using seven acute kidney injury (AKI) prediction models developed in MIMIC-IV and externally validated in MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD (116,010 patients in total). Additional simulations examined the effects of competing deaths and early censoring on BRII and conventional model performance metrics. Results: For 48-hour AKI prediction in the top 10% risk stratum, BRII ranged from 0.90 to 0.96 in MIMIC-III, compared with less than 0.26 across all models in eICU-CRD, where 61.5% of evaluated patients were censored before the prediction horizon. In the eICU-CRD top 10% strata for the same target, 37.0% to 50.2% of patients were censored early, 12.2% to 15.5% had AKI, and 3.4% to 8.1% died before AKI. BRII and PPV ordered at least one model pair differently in 34 of 48 cohort-outcome-top-k groups. Under simulated random censoring for 48-hour AKI prediction, BRII declined by up to 0.80 while binary-label AUROC changed by less than 0.02. Conclusions: BRII provided complementary information on high-risk stratum composition, yielding different model rankings from PPV and revealing substantial differences across external validation cohorts. Interpreted alongside PPV and its component decomposition, BRII offers a standardized approach to evaluating clinical prediction alerts across models and observation environments.

title: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Predict Dental Crowding in Modern Orthodontic Practice: A Comprehensive Review.
source: PubMed · The Kaohsiung journal of medical sciences
desc: [The Kaohsiung journal of medical sciences] Dental crowding is fundamental to orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning, yet what constitutes "crowding" remains surprisingly heterogeneous. Space analysis quantifies tooth size-arch length discrepancy, irregularity indices characterize alignment displacement, and clinician-assigned severity reflects broader diagnostic interpretation. This narrative review examines the evolution of crowding assessment from conventional space analysis and digital measurement to two-dimensional artificial intelligence (AI), three-dimensional point-cloud learning, and clinician-aware agentic AI. Digitalization improves efficiency and reproducibility but does not resolve fundamental dependencies on how crowding is defined, anatomically represented, and established as a reference standard. Two-dimensional models enable prediction from readily available images but are constrained by projection and scale, whereas three-dimensional approaches directly learn from dental surface representations and can capture local geometric relationships. In a companion study of 495 arches from 284 patients, PointNet++ achieved an R2 of 0.718 and a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.54 mm for prediction of crowding. In a separate retrospective demonstration, a bounded Gemini-based Agent incorporating matched record-derived verbal information reduced MAE from 1.951 to 1.437 mm, whereas mismatched information degraded performance. These findings also illustrate that the target construct-the specific clinical feature of crowding that a model is trained to predict-may differ across assessment methods. Together, these findings highlight a fundamental challenge: improving prediction does not resolve ambiguity in the target construct. Future crowding AI should therefore align the target construct, reference standard, and input representation; preserve provenance and uncertainty; integrate complementary clinical information transparently; and route uncertain cases for expert review.

Real-world, digital-first delivery of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in women
desc: At 6 months, a cohort of 8,127 women in the UK initiating GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy via a digital platform showed mean weight reduction comparable to that in randomized clinical trials. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated substantial weight reduction and cardiometabolic benefit in randomized trials; however, prospective implementation evidence from digital care models and female sex community populations remains limited. Here we report outcomes from an observational study of 8,127 women initiating GLP-1RA therapy (99.8% tirzepatide) through a structured digital program incorporating mandatory biochemical monitoring, weekly video-supported follow-up and clinician-guided dose titration in the UK. Mean weight reduction was 16.1 kg (95% confidence interval 15.9 to 16.2; P < 0.001), representing 15.5% of baseline weight; 83.1% achieved ≥10% and 22.4% achieved ≥20% weight loss, with consistent responses across age, baseline weight and socioeconomic strata. Among participants with paired biomarker data, mean glycated hemoglobin decreased by 3.3 mmol mol^−^1 (95% confidence interval 3.1 to 3.4; P < 0.001), normalizing in 84.5% of those with baseline diabetes-range values and 96.3% with prediabetes, and lipid parameters improved significantly (reductions in total cholesterol of 0.77 mmol l^−^1, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol of 0.61 mmol l^−^1 and triglycerides of 0.47 mmol l^−^1). Retention was 91.4% at 6 months, with no serious treatment-related adverse events. These findings support the feasibility of delivering structured, digitally enabled obesity pharmacotherapy at scale and provide prospective real-world implementation evidence for this care model. Interpretation is limited by the observational design, absence of a comparator group, self-pay population and 6-month follow-up.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Emergency Medical Call-Taking and Dispatch Operations: A Scoping Review.
desc: [Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland)] Objective: This study aimed to systematically review worldwide research on artificial intelligence (AI) applications in emergency medical service (EMS) call-taking and dispatch operations and identify current research trends and research needs. Methods: This scoping review was reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, KoreaMed, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library were searched for studies published from January 2021 to August 2026. Data were synthesized descriptively. Results: Eighteen studies from 13 countries and one multinational setting were included; eight (44.4%) were conducted in Europe. Patient Recognition and Classification was the predominant domain (11/18, 61.1%), followed by Dispatch Support and Operational Decision-Making (5/18, 27.8%) and Other Methodological Applications (2/18, 11.1%). Structured clinical or dispatch data were used in 11 studies, textual data in eight, and call audio in five; four applied multimodal integration. Deep learning (DL) was used as a primary model in 11 studies and classical machine learning (ML) in eight, including three using both; large language models (LLMs) were used in two. Eleven studies involved retrospective model development and internal validation, whereas only two were randomized controlled trials. None of the 11 model-development studies conducted independent external validation or calibration assessment, and the two randomized trials, one with high risk of bias and the other with some concerns, showed no consistent improvement across dispatch outcomes. Conclusions: AI applications span diverse clinical and operational tasks, with multimodal integration, speech technologies, and LLMs broadening their potential scope. Evidence remains dominated by retrospective model development and internal validation; prospective and real-world implementation studies are needed to establish safety and clinical utility before integration into EMS systems.

Artificial Intelligence for Thyroid Nodule Diagnosis: From Multimodal Integration to Clinical Utility.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Artificial intelligence (AI) for thyroid nodules should be evaluated against the decisions it changes, not diagnostic accuracy alone. This critical narrative review examines ultrasound, cytology, histology, and molecular models and distinguishes modality-specific prediction from implemented multimodal learning. The original PubMed/MEDLINE search through 10 August 2026 was supplemented on 25 September 2026 by targeted OpenAlex searches and checks of primary publications, reporting standards, and regulatory sources. Selected studies are compared by sample size, reference standard, acquisition setting, testing design, and performance with confidence intervals where available. We explain feature concatenation, intermediate representation learning, cross-attention, and decision-level fusion, and examine whether integration improves on the strongest component. Reported gains are inconsistent, and complete-case multimodal datasets may exclude the low-risk nodules most relevant to avoiding biopsy. High discrimination for histological malignancy or occult nodal disease does not demonstrate reduced overdiagnosis, fewer operations, or improved survival. A thyroid-specific translation roadmap therefore addresses active surveillance, partial verification and spectrum bias, Hashimoto thyroiditis and multinodular disease, cytology preparation shifts, category-specific thresholds, operator dependence, reporting frameworks, and regulatory change control. The priority is a calibrated, externally tested tool using information available at a defined clinical decision, followed by prospective evaluation of patient and workflow outcomes. A unified imaging-pathology-omics system and reliable AI prediction of surveillance progression remain research objectives rather than established clinical capabilities.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Gastroenterology: Towards Explainable, Generalisable and Clinically Actionable Decision Support.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in gastroenterology for endoscopic detection and characterisation, disease-activity assessment, risk prediction, treatment-response estimation and workflow support. However, high retrospective accuracy does not necessarily translate into reliable or beneficial clinical decision support. This structured narrative review examines the clinical development of artificial intelligence across gastrointestinal endoscopy, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary diseases through three translational dimensions: explainability, generalisability and clinical actionability. Communication, human oversight and lifecycle governance are considered cross-cutting determinants of implementation. The evidence is most mature in gastrointestinal endoscopy, particularly for computer-aided polyp detection, although benefits vary across operators, indications and practice settings. Applications in inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary care remain predominantly retrospective, with limited prospective evidence that model outputs alter management or improve patient outcomes. Explainability is commonly represented by heatmaps or feature-attribution methods, but rarely evaluated in terms of clinician understanding, calibrated trust or patient communication. External validation is becoming more frequent, yet geographic and technological transportability, calibration and performance under dataset shift remain insufficiently assessed. Prospective implementation and health-economic studies are uncommon, and available economic evidence is largely model-based. Clinical artificial intelligence should therefore be evaluated as a sociotechnical intervention comprising the model, interface, users, workflow, communication process and associated care pathway. Translation requires clinically defined use cases, representative multicentre validation, human-centred evaluation, prospective assessment of benefits and harms, and continuous post-deployment surveillance. Clinical AI in gastroenterology should complement clinical expertise through transparent, contestable and continuously monitored decision support that preserves clinician accountability and supports informed, patient-centred decisions.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Gingival Recession Assessment and Treatment Planning: A Scoping Review.
desc: [Journal of clinical medicine] Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly used in periodontal assessment, image analysis, outcome prediction, and clinical decision support. However, evidence specifically addressing gingival recession (GR) and related periodontal soft-tissue parameters remains fragmented and predominantly technical. This scoping review aimed to map AI/ML applications for the detection, measurement, prediction, and treatment planning of GR and to identify methodological limitations and translational evidence gaps. Methods: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and reported according to PRISMA-ScR. Eligibility was structured according to the Population-Concept-Context framework and included English-language original studies involving human participants or human-derived clinical data and evaluating AI/ML approaches directly related to GR or to periodontal soft-tissue or anatomical parameters relevant to its assessment or management. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Embase were utilized as the core bibliographic databases, while Google Scholar was used as an additional search source with screening restricted to the first 200 results ranked by relevance. No restrictions on publication year or start date were applied. Study characteristics, AI methods, clinical applications, validation strategies, and performance metrics were charted and descriptively synthesized. Results: Twelve studies were included across four main clinical domains: detection and segmentation of gingival recession and related soft-tissue features, measurement and anatomical landmark localization, prediction and risk assessment, and treatment planning or clinical decision support. AI/ML models generally demonstrated promising technical performance, including high classification and segmentation accuracy and submillimeter localization of periodontal anatomical landmarks. However, datasets, reference standards, validation strategies, and reported performance metrics were heterogeneous. Independent external validation remained limited, and most studies assessed technical performance rather than clinical utility. No study prospectively demonstrated that AI-assisted assessment or decision support improved clinician decision-making or patient outcomes. Conclusions: AI shows potential to support objective GR assessment, prediction, and treatment planning in gingival recession management. However, current evidence r

title: Multimodal artificial intelligence to predict cardiomyopathy development in hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis.
desc: [Open heart] Hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRv) is a rare multisystem disorder with marked phenotypic heterogeneity. Cardiac involvement, a major prognostic determinant, often develops years after neurological onset and remains clinically silent in early stages, delaying diagnosis and treatment. We developed a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) model integrating clinical, electrocardiographic and echocardiographic data to predict cardiomyopathy in patients with ATTRv but without baseline cardiac involvement. Adult patients with genetically confirmed ATTRv amyloidosis evaluated at four Italian tertiary referral centres between 2011 and 2026 were retrospectively included. Only patients without evidence of cardiac involvement at baseline were eligible. A machine learning model was developed using structured clinical variables, while deep learning models were trained on electrocardiographic and echocardiographic data. These models were integrated into a multimodal ensemble framework. Primary endpoint was development of ATTRv cardiomyopathy (ATTRv-CM), defined as scintigraphy-based diagnostic criteria for ATTR-CM in the absence of monoclonal gammopathy and evidence of left ventricular maximal wall thickness exceeding 12 mm. The cohort included 97 patients (63 mutation carriers and 34 with only mild neurological involvement). Over a mean follow-up of 2.5±2.2 years (IQR 1–3), 15 patients developed cardiomyopathy. Unimodal models showed good predictive performance (all training set area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) in the range of 0.86–0.94, all test set AUC within 0.74–0.89). The multimodal ensemble achieved optimal performance, with 100% accuracy and an F1 score of 1.0, in predicting ATTR-CM. Multimodal AI enables early prediction of cardiac involvement in ATTRv, supporting personalised surveillance and optimised clinical management.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Novel Therapeutic Opportunities in Precision Oncology.
source: PubMed · International journal of molecular sciences
desc: [International journal of molecular sciences] Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping molecular oncology by making complex biological data tractable and by extending the reach of precision drug discovery. Its emerging value is particularly evident at the interface of immunoengineering and targeted therapy, where computational models can help prioritize tumor-selective antigens, predict neoantigen immunogenicity, optimize engineered receptors, support antibody and antibody-drug conjugate design, guide small-molecule discovery, refine genome-editing strategies, and anticipate treatment response. Across these applications, the central promise is not automation for its own sake, but a wider therapeutic window in which tumor control is increased while off-target toxicity is reduced. Yet the translational gap remains substantial. Many models are still preclinical, external validation is limited, and clinical implementation remains uncommon. This Commentary follows representative methods across a therapeutic continuum that now extends from target discovery and therapeutic engineering to imaging, liquid biopsy, resistance forecasting, combination selection, and drug repurposing. We argue that clinical value will depend on closed-loop workflows in which multimodal predictions are experimentally validated, externally tested, and longitudinally updated to guide the next therapeutic decision.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Spirometry in Primary Healthcare: Opportunities for Early Detection of Small Airway Dysfunction.
desc: [Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland)] Spirometry underuse and persistent limitations in its technical quality and interpretation in primary healthcare (PHC) contribute to delayed and inaccurate diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma. Artificial intelligence (AI) has recently demonstrated, at the randomised controlled trial level, that it can improve spirometry interpretation by primary care clinicians. Maximal mid-expiratory flow (MMEF), a spirometric measure routinely derived from every forced expiratory manoeuvre, has been associated with subsequent airflow obstruction and lung function decline, particularly when conventional spirometric indices remain preserved, suggesting that it may contribute to earlier recognition of small airway dysfunction. However, no existing review has examined whether AI could specifically address the challenge of MMEF interpretation, and the incremental value of MMEF within AI-assisted spirometry models remains unestablished. This narrative review synthesises current evidence on AI-assisted spirometry in PHC across three evidence domains, diagnostic classification, quality control, and computational small airway assessment, and examines the potential for integrating MMEF with conventional spirometric indices, flow-volume curve morphology, technical quality, clinical characteristics, and longitudinal data to support its clinical interpretation. The available evidence supports the feasibility of the individual components underpinning this proposed framework, including AI-assisted spirometry interpretation, automated quality assessment, and computational extraction of small airway information from spirometric data. However, the contextual integration of MMEF within AI-assisted models has not yet been prospectively evaluated, and validation of its incremental predictive value and clinical utility is needed before implementation can be recommended.

title: Deep learning reconstruction in prostate MRI: technical principles, clinical applications, and future directions.
desc: [Abdominal radiology (New York)] Multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) has become integral to the detection, localization, risk stratification, and management of prostate cancer. Increasing utilization of prostate MRI in screening, active surveillance, targeted biopsy guidance, and treatment planning has amplified the demand for faster imaging protocols while maintaining high diagnostic quality. Conventional MRI acceleration strategies, including parallel imaging and compressed sensing, improve acquisition efficiency but remain limited by trade-offs involving signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), image sharpness, artifacts, and reconstruction complexity. Deep learning reconstruction (DLR) has emerged as a promising artificial intelligence-based approach for MRI acceleration and image enhancement. Unlike traditional reconstruction methods that rely primarily on predefined mathematical models, DLR uses neural networks to learn image priors and reconstruction features from MRI data. Published studies suggest that DLR may enable accelerated acquisitions while maintaining or, in some settings, improving image quality through denoising, artifact reduction, and improved spatial resolution and lesion conspicuity. However, these effects vary according to the reconstruction algorithm, sequence, acceleration factor, and clinical setting. Variational networks combine physics-based MRI constraints with learned regularization and represent an important framework for DLR. In prostate MRI, available studies have reported substantial reductions in acquisition time for T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted imaging while generally maintaining perceived image quality. Reported benefits include improved lesion conspicuity, reader confidence, and delineation of anatomic structures. Current evidence suggests that DLR generally preserves PI-RADS assessment and diagnostic performance rather than systematically altering lesion categorization; however, evidence demonstrating improvements in diagnostic accuracy or clinical outcomes remains limited. Important limitations include vendor and algorithm dependence, potential reconstruction artifacts, variability in quantitative imaging metrics, limited multicenter validation, and uncertain generalizability across scanners, protocols, and clinical settings. This review summarizes the technical principles underlying DLR, discusses current clinical applications in prostate MRI, highlights representative studies and workflow implications, reviews limitations, and outlines f

title: Large Language Models in the Emergency Department: Fairness Implications for Clinicians.
source: PubMed · Clinical and experimental emergency medicine
desc: [Clinical and experimental emergency medicine] Applications of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), are rapidly expanding in emergency medicine, but concerns remain regarding their fairness across diverse patient populations. Fairness extends beyond model accuracy and includes equal performance across patient groups, equitable outcomes and allocation of clinical benefits, and procedural fairness throughout the lifecycle of AI implementation. This narrative review aims to provide a practical framework for understanding and evaluating fairness in emergency medicine applications of AI and LLMs. This narrative review organizes fairness risks into three clinically relevant layers. First, datalevel fairness concerns the data used to train, fine-tune, or prompt AI systems. Biased clinical data, including non-random missingness and stigmatizing documentation, can influence model performance. Second, output-level fairness concerns whether the outputs generated by AI systems are equally accurate, safe, and useful across patient groups. In emergency care, subgroup-specific errors in recommendations, predictions, translations, or instructions may arise from aggregation, learning, or evaluation bias, even when overall model performance appears strong. Third, human-interaction fairness concerns whether the benefits of AI are realized equitably in clinical practice and by patients. Even when data and outputs are fair, inequities may arise if clinicians over-rely on or reject useful AI recommendations, or if patients are unable to access, understand, or trust AI-mediated information. Clinicians should consider potential implications for safety, transparency, and fairness alongside overall model accuracy when evaluating AI tools in emergency medicine.

title: Navigating the Regulatory Landscape of Artificial Intelligence in Australian Clinical Dentistry.
desc: [Australian dental journal] Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming clinical dentistry, with an increasing number of AI-powered diagnostic and treatment planning tools entering the Australian healthcare market. As clinicians adopt AI-based dental software, it is becoming increasingly important to understand the regulatory frameworks that govern them. This narrative review explores the regulatory approval pathways and governance of AI tools used in Australian dental and healthcare settings to inform and educate practitioners. Australia regulates AI-based dental software primarily through the Therapeutic Goods Administration, which classifies eligible products as software as a medical device under a risk-based, technology-agnostic framework established by the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989. AI tools that function as clinical decision-support systems are subject to mandatory conformity assessment and registration on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) prior to lawful supply. Although the Australian framework aligns with the International Medical Device Regulators Forum principles, the approval process is comparatively less transparent than that required in jurisdictions such as the United States and the European Union, and questions remain regarding the consistency of post-market oversight. This review also highlights emerging regulatory challenges associated with adaptive AI systems. Software could initially receive approval as a low-risk device that evolves to provide specific clinical advice beyond its approval scope. These updates to functionality risk bypassing established oversight pathways that rely on self-reported intended use. Furthermore, currently available AI tools lack comprehensive public-facing transparent evidence for regulatory compliance that is complicated by ambiguous and inconsistent terminology and adaptive AI system classification. Regardless of regulatory approval, clinicians remain professionally accountable for the use of AI tools in clinical decision-making and for ensuring that patient care meets accepted standards of practice.

title: Artificial Intelligence Applications for Composite Materials: A Review.
desc: [Polymers] Composite materials are not easy to model using traditional experiments and physics-based approaches due to their diverse properties and multiscale nature. This review summarizes how artificial intelligence (AI) methodologies, including machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI, have been increasingly transforming and how they have been increasingly applied to composite materials research. It combines their possible use across the prediction of their properties, damage detection, structural health monitoring, and materials design. Searches were performed in Scopus and Google Scholar for articles published using combined keywords such as "(artificial intelligence OR machine learning OR deep learning OR Generative AI) AND (composite OR fiber reinforced) AND (prediction OR optimization OR characterization)". The search strategy was designed to capture both fundamental developments in AI methodologies relevant to materials research and their specific applications to composite materials. The identified publications underwent a two-step selection process: (i) an initial review of titles and abstracts, and (ii) a detailed full-text evaluation. Studies were included if they provided explicit descriptions of AI models, clearly specified datasets, and applied quantitative performance assessments to composite materials-related applications such as material property prediction, damage detection, characterization, or manufacturing process optimization. For each selected article, relevant information was extracted in a structured and consistent manner, including the type of composite material, AI methodology, input parameters, dataset characteristics and size, validation methods, and application domain. These data were used to support both quantitative trend analysis and the qualitative identification of research gaps and future research opportunities in composite materials research. Supervised learning methods, in particular artificial neural networks, support vector machines, random forests, and decision trees, were commonly used and exhibited durable potential accuracy in predicting properties of composite materials. Unsupervised methods such as principal component analysis (PCA) and clustering were comparatively underused. Generative AI, including generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs), and physics-informed models emerged as growing approaches for synthetic data generation and improved interpretability, respectively. The

title: Large language model assistance for report-based carotid plaque AHA classification: a multi-reader study.
desc: [Insights into imaging] To evaluate whether large language model assistance improves radiologists' agreement with a text-based reference standard in inferring the modified American Heart Association carotid plaque classification from free-text MRI reports, and whether a lightweight model can perform well under criteria-guided prompting. This retrospective study included 433 patients from three institutions. In a report-based reader study, four radiologists classified MRI reports with and without large language model assistance. In standalone evaluation, a rule-based baseline and 10 models were compared under naive and criteria-guided prompting. The reference standard was expert consensus based on the report text. Among 433 patients (mean age, 65.9 years ± 13.4; 248 males), AI assistance improved six-class agreement with the text-based reference standard. At the vessel level, junior radiologists improved from 61.75% to 83.12% (Qwen3-8B) and 87.75% (DeepSeek-R1); senior radiologists from 77.00% to 87.50% and 92.25%, respectively (all Holm-corrected p < 0.001). Patient-level agreement increased from 41.0% to 78.8% (junior) and from 59.8% to 87.8% (senior) with DeepSeek-R1. Agreement increased (quadratic-weighted κ: 0.231 without AI vs 0.775 with DeepSeek-R1). In standalone evaluation, criteria-guided prompting improved Qwen3-8B agreement from 38.91% to 81.52% (95% CI: 78.87-84.06%), remaining 5.89 percentage points below DeepSeek-R1 (87.41%; 95% CI: 85.10-89.61%). In this report-based classification setting, large language model assistance improved radiologists' agreement with the text-based reference standard, with larger gains in junior radiologists. When prompts explicitly encoded AHA criteria, an 8B local candidate model performed well, supporting its potential use as a standardization aid for text-based workflows. Question Report-based modified AHA classification of carotid plaques is experience-dependent and difficult to standardize, as mapping multi-sequence imaging findings to classification conclusions imposes substantial cognitive load. Findings Large language model assistance improved agreement with a text-based reference standard and raised inter-reader consistency (weighted κ 0.231-0.775), narrowing the junior-senior gap. Critical relevance statement Embedding explicit AHA criteria in the prompt let an 8B model approach 671B-model agreement (38.91-81.52%), supporting standardized text-based workflows without fine-tuning.

title: Large Language Model-Assisted Review of Clinical Trial Informed Consent for Data Reuse: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Approach.
desc: [JMIR medical informatics] Regulatory frameworks such as the Belmont Report, the Common Rule, and the Declaration of Helsinki require informed consent to ensure participants understand a study's purpose and can make voluntary decisions about their involvement. Regulations, including the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation [EU] 2016/679), further emphasize that consent must be freely given and revocable without disadvantage. Although informed consent forms (ICFs) are intended to be clear and accessible, they have become increasingly lengthy and complex. Large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to navigate and interpret this complexity and have shown promise in biomedical information extraction tasks. However, their susceptibility to hallucinations limits their reliability in high-stakes settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can mitigate such errors. This study evaluates the integration of GPT-4.1 with RAG for reviewing data reuse language in ICFs and its ability to interpret complex ICF language. First, we processed 438 ICFs from different trials, including multiple countries, languages, and versions of ICFs. Using expertly curated prompts, we extracted information about data reuse using GPT-4.1. By comparing the LLM-generated data reuse outputs with human expert ground truth, we evaluated accuracy and the time required to extract information for each ICF. To further validate the workflow, we evaluated an independent set of 488 ICFs spanning additional trials, languages, and regions. During the validation phase, the workflow was evaluated using a baseline assessment (89 ICFs) followed by 3 iterative optimization rounds assessed on 14, 281, and 104 ICFs, respectively. For this cohort, we assessed the correctness of LLM outputs along with the quality of supporting evidence provided by the model. Across the initial set of 438 ICFs, the system achieved 81.6% accuracy. During validation, the baseline accuracy using the preoptimized prompts was 84.0% (89 documents). Accuracy improved sequentially across the 3 iterative optimization rounds, increasing from 82.3% in the first round (14 documents) to 90.7% in the second round (281 documents), and reaching 92.1% in the third and final round on an independent holdout cohort of 104 documents. Ultimately, using our RAG-based approach, the system accurately extracted data reuse information across multiple languages. Our RAG-based workflow demonstrated the ability to effectively support the ICF review process for data re

title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence and Multicenter Real-World Evidence to Advance Precision Dosing: A Critical Perspective Review.
desc: [Therapeutic drug monitoring] Precision dosing integrates patient-specific factors to optimize pharmacotherapy. However, current evidence often relies on limited single-center studies, restricting generalizability. A narrative review of literature on real-world evidence, pharmacogenetics, biomarkers, artificial intelligence (AI), and privacy-preserving data strategies relevant to precision dosing was conducted. Single-center data are insufficient for robust precision-dosing evidence because of small subgroups and local practice biases. Multicenter privacy-preserving systems enable richer, more generalizable datasets that link doses, exposures, genotypes, biomarkers, and outcomes. However, multicenter collaborations should remain aligned with the intended population and should not imply indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous data. Secure pooled environments, federated learning, and synthetic data play distinct method-dependent roles. AI supports exposure estimation, phenotype extraction, and modeling of complex relationships but requires rigorous validation against conventional methods. Causal inference requires epidemiological rigor beyond predictive performance. Advancing precision dosing requires multicenter, purpose-specific, privacy-preserving, methodologically rigorous, and clinically validated data systems guided by clinical pharmacologists, with AI serving as a complementary tool rather than a default solution.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Plant Gene Regulatory Networks.
source: PubMed · International journal of molecular sciences
desc: [International journal of molecular sciences] Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are the maps that plant biologists most want to draw, with arrows pointing from transcription factors to the genes they control, explaining how plants develop and respond to the environment. Since experimental validation of even one arrow can take years, and a single plant genome harbours tens of millions of candidate TF-target pairs, this gap has driven the development of numerous computational methods for GRN inference. Here I review three generations of computational approaches to plant GRN inference and measure them against a five-level ladder of evidence, including statistical association, conditional dependence, physical binding, functional regulation and causal circuits. Classical statistics and machine learning have simplified complex gene expression data into clear, prioritised predictions. Techniques like single-cell and multi-omics methods help uncover cell type-specific networks based on chromatin accessibility and binding motifs. Now, deep learning can interpret cis-regulatory grammar directly from genome sequences, and foundation models trained on plant genomes and millions of cells hold exciting potential to share regulatory insights across different species. The most promising route forward is a lab-in-the-loop division of labour in which foundation models serve not as oracles but as hypothesis engines, collapsing fifty million candidate TF-target pairs into the few hundred edges most worth the bench's time, with each round of validation sharpening the next round of prediction.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Sensing Technologies for Vascular Access in Hemodialysis: A Narrative Review.
desc: [Sensors (Basel, Switzerland)] Vascular access performance determines the adequacy, safety, and cost of hemodialysis. Stenosis, thrombosis, cannulation difficulty, infection, and access-related cardiac stress remain major sources of morbidity. This narrative review examines artificial intelligence and sensing technologies for vascular access care, based on PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov searches through 22 August 2026 with citation chaining. Existing reviews have examined artificial intelligence in dialysis broadly or prediction models in isolation. In this review, the vascular access itself is kept as the unit of analysis, and the evidence is followed across four connected stages: systemic risk stratification; prediction of maturation, dysfunction, and complications from clinical, ultrasound, and multimodal data; longitudinal monitoring with optical, acoustic, vibration, thermal, and pressure sensors; and procedural support with robotics and visualization technologies. Reported discrimination is high in retrospective, recording-level analyses, reaching areas under the curve of 0.99 and sample-level accuracy of 100%, but falls to approximately 0.71 in longitudinal designs that predict future events in the same patients; patient-level external validation and calibration are also rarely reported. No approach has yet been demonstrated to reduce thrombosis, prolong patency, avoid interventions, or lower cost relative to standard care in prospective multicenter studies. Deployment is further constrained by power budgets, duty cycling, and transmission bandwidth in wearable devices. Technical feasibility should not be read as clinical utility.

title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in the Process of Power Cable Operation and Maintenance: A Review.
desc: [Sensors (Basel, Switzerland)] Power cables are the core power transmission carriers for modern urban power supply, and their safe and reliable operation is crucial to the stability of urban power grids. Traditional cable operation and maintenance (O&M) mainly relies on manual experience, suffers from prominent data silos, and struggles to meet the demands of complex power grids and high-reliability power supply. Data-driven artificial intelligence has been increasingly applied in cable O&M, serving as a complement to conventional operation frameworks. We focus on the O&M process oriented towards fault handling. Firstly, attention is paid to the core physical quantities for cable condition monitoring and the current application status of Internet of Things (IoT) sensing technology. Subsequently, the limitations of traditional fault diagnosis methods are systematically analyzed. Furthermore, we highlight the research progress of deep learning models such as attention mechanisms and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in cable fault diagnosis. Digital twin (DT) technology is also addressed, and its synergistic effect with AI technology in the intelligent O&M framework is systematically analyzed. Finally, we summarize the challenges faced in current technology implementation and look forward to future development directions.

title: Blepharoplasty in the Artificial Intelligence Era.
source: PubMed · Oral and maxillofacial surgery clinics of North America
desc: [Oral and maxillofacial surgery clinics of North America] Blepharoplasty and related periorbital procedures sit at the interface of functional reconstruction, esthetic surgery, ophthalmology, facial plastic surgery, and oral and maxillofacial surgery. Because eyelid and periorbital changes can be captured in photographs, videos, and 3-dimensional imaging, artificial intelligence has growing relevance for objective measurement, screening, planning, outcome assessment, and patient education. Current evidence is promising but heterogeneous. Image-based computer vision and deep learning appear closest to clinical use, whereas large language and generative image models require careful oversight. This review summarizes practical applications and proposes a cautious implementation pathway.

title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Subjective Workload Among Clinical Nurses: A Cross-Sectional Study.
desc: [Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland)] Background: Although artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into nursing practice, little is known about the association between nurses' AI literacy and their subjective workload. This study examines the associations between three dimensions of AI literacy-technical understanding, critical appraisal, and practical application-and overall and dimension-specific subjective workload among clinical nurses. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 305 clinical nurses recruited through convenience sampling from two hospitals in central Taiwan. AI literacy was assessed using the self-report Scale for the Assessment of Non-Experts' AI Literacy (SNAIL), with responses rated on a five-point Likert scale. Subjective workload was assessed using the self-report NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). Pearson correlation and hierarchical multiple linear regression analyses were performed, adjusting for relevant demographic and work-related characteristics. Results: Higher technical understanding, critical appraisal, and practical application were each associated with lower temporal demand and frustration, and these associations remained statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. More limited associations were observed for physical demand and the overall NASA-TLX workload score, while no robust associations were found for mental demand, effort, or performance. Conclusions: The assessed dimensions of AI literacy are found to be associated with specific dimensions of nurses' subjective workload, rather than with workload uniformly, with the clearest relationships observed for temporal demand and frustration. Further longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to determine whether improvements in AI literacy are accompanied by meaningful changes in nurses' workload experiences.

title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Access Reproductive Healthcare Information by U.S. States Following Sexual Assault.
desc: [Archives of sexual behavior] There is currently wide variability across U.S. states regarding the legality of abortion with some states having relatively open access to abortion services and others with a total or near total ban on abortion access. Further complicating these state-by-state differences is the variability in policies and procedures with regard to exemptions (e.g., rape, incest) that may allow women access to abortion services that otherwise would be banned in that state. Factors such as a victim's alcohol use at the time of rape and victim's rape acknowledgment may delay or prevent women from seeking medical care post-assault. To help navigate potential confusion regarding state-level policies and requirements to access abortion services following a rape in which they became pregnant, women may use Artificial Intelligence tools, including ChatGPT, for reproductive health care information. Thus, we sought to qualitatively examine information provided by ChatGPT-4o to women seeking information on how to access abortions in each state depending on their alcohol use and rape acknowledgment after finding out they are pregnant following a rape. Using data collected between October 31 and November 11, 2024, we systematically analyzed ChatGPT-4o's responses to abortion access requests across all 50 U.S. states using four prompts that varied by alcohol use and rape acknowledgment, and qualitatively coded responses for accuracy, helpfulness, and inclusion of empathic statements. Results revealed no significant differences in ChatGPT-4o responses across prompt conditions and one difference based on U.S. state level abortion access restriction. Responses in states with more severe restrictions were more likely to include information on rape exemptions than states with less restrictions in abortion access. However, responses often failed to include helpful information and statements reflective of empathic tone, which may exacerbate pre-existing disparities across U.S. states.

title: Reference Standards in Artificial Intelligence Detection of Apical Periodontitis: A Narrative Review of What Reported Accuracy Measures.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] The accuracy reported for detecting apical periodontitis using artificial intelligence (AI) is generally interpreted as accuracy against the disease; however, this is usually not the case. Compared with histopathology, single-view periapical radiography detects 16 to 27% of confirmed lesions and 38% with parallax, with a pooled digital sensitivity of 61.0% and a negative predictive value of 41.6%. Two blinded specialists reading 1717 radiographs disagreed on 22% of teeth. Detection depended on lesion size and site: simulated cancellous-bone lesions were invisible below 1 mm in incisors and 3 mm in molars. Of the 44 primary studies identified, 34 (77%) used a label that was a reading of the index image or was unascertainable; eight (18%) used an independent reference-six (14%) suited to contemporaneous detection and two to later treatment outcomes. No cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) input study had a reference independent of its volume. One commercial platform reported 92.3% sensitivity against same-image consensus and 47.9% against blinded CBCT. The reported accuracy is thus in agreement with a noisy rater; recognising this changes what meta-analyses pool. A model that reproduces human labels would have a lower sensitivity against disease than reported; for real-world models, the direction depends on error dependence that the study design cannot identify.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Facial Analysis/Facial Nerve/Facial Palsy.
source: PubMed · Oral and maxillofacial surgery clinics of North America
desc: [Oral and maxillofacial surgery clinics of North America] Artificial intelligence (AI)-based facial analysis enables objective and quantitative evaluation of facial morphology. Recent advances in computer vision allow automated detection of facial landmarks and reproducible measurement of facial symmetry, movement, and emotional expression. Several AI systems, including Emotrics, MediaPipe Face Mesh, Real-Time Facial Asymmetry Analysis, FaceReader, and Affdex, have been applied to outcome assessment after facial reanimation procedures and facial nerve reconstruction. Similar computational approaches can also be applied to evaluate structural facial deformities, such as those observed after mandibular reconstruction. By reducing subjective bias and improving reproducibility, AI-based facial analysis may support more evidence-based evaluation of reconstructive surgical outcomes.

title: Curriculum-Based Deep Learning for Automated Segmental Left Ventricular Hypertrophy Classification Using Short-Axis Echocardiography.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Background: Accurate detection and classification of segmental left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) are challenging due to rib and reverberation artifacts in two-dimensional short-axis (2D-SAX) echocardiography view. These artifacts lead to ambiguity in the boundaries of the myocardial region. Existing artificial intelligence techniques focus on global LVH detection compared to segmental LVH classification. Methodology: To solve the abovementioned problem, a curriculum-based left ventricular hypertrophy deep learning (LVH-DL) framework is proposed for segmental LVH classification. The proposed framework was tested with 2000 images of segmental LVH, which consists of (a) apical-423, (b) basal-382, (c) mid-ventricular-349, (d) diffuse-453, and (e) normal-393. The curriculum-based deep learning model consists of proposed algorithms such as (i) preprocessing of Mountaineering-Team-Based Optimization Deep Denoised Convolutional Neural Network (MTBO-DnCNN) for removing artifacts and enhancing the boundaries, (ii) segmentation of modified active contour segmentation (MACS) algorithm accurately extracting the myocardium region from the background, and (iii) classification of curriculum-based ConvNeXt-V2 model classifying segmental LVH using inter-channel features such as valvular structures and chamber size from the segmented myocardial region. Results: The proposed LVH-DL framework achieves a classification accuracy of about (a) 96.5% for apical, (b) 95% for basal, (c) 95.8% for mid-ventricular, (d) 97.2% for diffuse, and (e) 95% for normal. Conclusions: Thus, Thus, the proposed LVH-DL framework acts as a decision support tool for early identification of segmental LVH.

title: Artificial Intelligence Powered End-to-End Agricultural Machinery: Intelligent Transformation of Design and Maintenance Systems.
desc: [Sensors (Basel, Switzerland)] Reliable condition monitoring and fault diagnosis in agricultural machinery depend on interpreting sensor measurements under variable field conditions. Noise, occlusion, changing loads, and sensor degradation can obscure relevant features, while complementary measurements offer opportunities to reduce information gaps. This scoping review synthesizes 147 included evidence sources published from 2014 to early 2026, supplemented by 11 contextual publications. It examines sensing, feature extraction, and information fusion across mechanical modeling and design, perception, automation and control, and operation and maintenance. Modeling and design provide physical context for interpreting measurements, while perception and control connect state estimation with operational feedback. Applications in blockage detection and multi-component monitoring illustrate how complementary signals can support abnormal-state identification and operational intervention. However, improvements in perception accuracy or control performance do not independently establish improved fault diagnosis. Reported results often depend on local datasets or controlled platforms, and calibration errors, temporal misalignment, and changing operating conditions can compromise fused estimates. Evidence for reliable early warning, precise fault localization, and diagnostic robustness under degraded sensing remains limited. Future evaluations should compare fused and individual-sensor inputs under matched conditions, including noise, partial sensor failure, and changes across machines and seasons. Linking these comparisons to false alarms, missed faults, warning lead time, and maintenance decisions is essential for establishing the practical contribution of sensor fusion.

title: Deep Learning and Domain Expertise for Fabricating High-Performance Biosensors.
desc: [ACS sensors] Transcription factor-based biosensors are essential for the scalable bioproduction of plant natural products. However, a major bottleneck in developing high-performance biosensors is the engineering of responsive promoters due to the vast sequence space and poorly understood sequence-function relationships. Here, we extend our previously published DeepSEED framework into an artificial intelligence-driven pipeline for efficient and extensible biosensor-responsive promoter optimization. This strategy integrates deep learning with domain-specific biological expertise. By fixing core promoter elements, varying the number and position of transcription factor binding sites (TFBSs) to define promoter backbones, and subsequently optimizing the flanking sequences, we enable the de novo design of promoters. We systematically apply this strategy to optimize a panel of biosensors across different transcription factors and regulatory modes, including four metabolite-responsive biosensors and a quorum-sensing-based environmental sensor. The resulting biosensors exhibit diverse dynamic behaviors with markedly improved sensitivity, expanded dynamic range, and increased maximum output. For instance, the optimized naringenin biosensor demonstrates a 32-fold broader dynamic range and a 27-fold higher maximum output compared to its parent. To illustrate its utility in metabolic engineering, we employed a DeepSEED-designed promoter to dynamically regulate a p-coumaric acid biosynthesis pathway, boosting production by 117.0%. Our work extends the previously published DeepSEED framework into a powerful pipeline for biosensor optimization and delivers a portfolio of high-performance regulatory elements, addressing a critical need and facilitating the development of more intelligent and productive metabolic engineering systems.
